usageSteps: Use the sliders on the left to set your current age (18-80) and target retirement age, your current investment portfolio, how much you save and invest each month, and your expected annual expenses in retirement. You can also fine-tune your expected real annual return (0-15%), safe withdrawal rate (2-6%), and effective tax rate in retirement (0-40%) to match your own investing style and tax situation. Choose from 5 currencies ($, €, £, ₩, ¥) to run the numbers in whichever unit makes sense for you.

As soon as you change an input, the result cards on the right instantly recalculate your FIRE number, the age you'll reach it, and the years remaining. The chart below separates the accumulation phase, while you're still saving, from the withdrawal phase, after you retire, using different colors, so you can see at a glance how your portfolio grows and then gets drawn down.

Turn on "Scenario A/B comparison" to enter two different saving strategies at once, for example a higher monthly contribution or a different target age, and see both paths plotted side by side on the chart and result cards. This makes it easy to see exactly how much sooner a small increase in savings could get you to FIRE, or how much a later target age would ease your monthly savings burden.

All calculations run instantly in your own browser, and nothing you enter, your age, assets, or income, is ever stored or sent to a server. Your FIRE number also isn't just annual expenses divided by the withdrawal rate: it's grossed up for the effective tax rate you set, so with the tax rate at 0% you'll see the classic "25x rule," and with a higher rate you'll see the larger target you'd actually need.

Faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
Faq.subtitle: Answers to common questions about the FIRE Calculator.

items.question: What is FIRE?
items.answer: FIRE stands for Financial Independence, Retire Early. It's the practice of aggressively saving and investing so your portfolio can cover your living expenses well before traditional retirement age.

items.question: How is my FIRE number calculated?
items.answer: Your FIRE number is your annual expenses divided by your chosen withdrawal rate (commonly 4%, i.e. multiplied by 25), then grossed up for the effective tax rate you set on withdrawals — a higher tax rate raises the target, since you need to withdraw more to keep the same after-tax spending power. With the tax rate set to 0%, this is simply expenses × 25. The calculator projects your savings growth year by year until that number is reached.

items.question: Is the 4% withdrawal rate always safe?
items.answer: The 4% rule is a widely used historical guideline, not a guarantee. Market returns, inflation, and your time horizon all affect how safe a given withdrawal rate really is, so treat the result as a planning estimate rather than a promise.

items.question: Do I need to create an account to use this calculator?
items.answer: No. The FIRE Calculator works entirely in your browser without sign-up — your inputs are not saved or sent to a server.

items.question: Can I compare two different savings scenarios?
items.answer: Yes. Use the Scenario A / B compare mode to adjust savings rate, returns, or expenses side by side and see how each path affects your FIRE date.

items.question: Which currencies are supported?
items.answer: You can switch the currency from the selector at the top of the calculator; the input ranges automatically rescale to match the selected currency.

items.question: Is this financial advice?
items.answer: No. This tool is for educational and illustrative purposes only and does not constitute financial, tax, or investment advice. Please consult a licensed professional for advice specific to your situation.

items.question: Is the FIRE Calculator free to use?
items.answer: Yes, it's completely free with no limits on how many scenarios you can run.

coast-fire.name: Coast FIRE
coast-fire.short: Find how much you need today to stop saving and still reach FIRE by retirement age.
coast-fire.title: Coast FIRE Calculator: When Can You Stop Saving?
coast-fire.description: Free Coast FIRE calculator: see how much you need invested today to stop saving and still reach your FIRE number by retirement age.
coast-fire.lead: Coast FIRE means you already have enough invested that, left alone, it will grow to your full FIRE number by a traditional retirement age. From that point you only need to earn enough to cover today's living costs. Enter your numbers to find your Coast number, your progress, and the age you could start coasting.
how: Your Coast number is the amount you would need today so that compound growth alone, with no further contributions, reaches your FIRE number at your chosen retirement age. The longer the runway and the higher the real return you assume, the smaller that number is.

The chart compares your portfolio, growing with your monthly contributions, against the Coast threshold, which rises each year as retirement gets closer. The first age where your line crosses the dashed line is the age you could stop contributing.
coast-fire.formula: Coast number = FIRE number ÷ (1 + real return) ^ years until retirement. FIRE number = annual expenses ÷ (1 − tax rate) ÷ withdrawal rate.
coast-fire.bestFor: Coast FIRE suits people who started investing early and want the freedom to take a lower-paying or more meaningful job now, knowing the long-term plan is already on track.
coast-fire.watchOut: The result depends heavily on the real return you assume and on markets cooperating. Trying a conservative return such as 4% to 5% shows how sensitive the plan is, and your expenses at retirement may differ from today's.

faq.question: What is the difference between Coast FIRE and regular FIRE?
faq.answer: Regular FIRE means you can stop working now because your portfolio covers your spending. Coast FIRE means you can stop saving now because growth alone will get you to FIRE by a later retirement age, but you still need income to pay for living costs until then.

faq.question: Which retirement age should I use?
faq.answer: Use the age at which you would like to start living off the portfolio, such as 55, 60, or 65. A later age gives compounding more time, so the Coast number is lower, while an earlier age raises it.

faq.question: Does Coast FIRE include Social Security or pensions?
faq.answer: No. The calculator leaves out state and employer pensions to stay conservative. If you expect them, lower your annual expenses input by the amount they would cover to see a smaller target.

barista-fire.name: Barista FIRE
barista-fire.short: See how part-time income shrinks the portfolio you need and how much sooner you can leave full-time work.
barista-fire.title: Barista FIRE Calculator: Part-Time Income + Portfolio
barista-fire.description: Free Barista FIRE calculator: see how part-time income lowers the portfolio you need and how many years earlier you can leave full-time work.
barista-fire.lead: Barista FIRE is a semi-retirement path: you leave full-time work earlier, and part-time or low-stress income covers part of your expenses while your portfolio covers the rest. Enter your spending and expected part-time income to see the smaller portfolio you need and how much sooner you can get there.
how: A Barista FIRE number only has to fund the gap between your annual expenses and your part-time income. Every unit of expenses covered by work is a unit your portfolio no longer has to produce, which at a 4% withdrawal rate means you need about 25 times that amount less in savings.

The chart shows your path to the Barista number with a dashed line for the full FIRE path, so you can see the years saved. Many people also choose part-time work for benefits such as health insurance, which is worth pricing separately.
barista-fire.formula: Barista number = (annual expenses − part-time income) ÷ (1 − tax rate) ÷ withdrawal rate.
barista-fire.bestFor: It suits people who would rather work fewer or more enjoyable hours than reach full retirement as fast as possible, and who are confident they can find steady part-time income.
barista-fire.watchOut: Part-time income is never guaranteed, health insurance can be a large cost in some countries, and the portfolio still has to survive market downturns. Treat the part-time income as a range, not a certainty.

faq.question: How much part-time income should I assume?
faq.answer: Use a conservative figure you could realistically earn after tax in a role you would not mind doing for years. Try a few amounts to see how sensitive the result is.

faq.question: Is the part-time income taxed in this calculator?
faq.answer: Enter it after tax. The tax rate field applies to withdrawals from the portfolio, not to the part-time income.

faq.question: What if I stop working part-time later?
faq.answer: Then your portfolio must cover the full expenses from that point. Compare the Barista number with the full FIRE number shown in the results to see how much more you would need, and keep growing the portfolio meanwhile.

lean-fire.name: Lean FIRE
lean-fire.short: Retire on a minimalist budget with a much smaller target.
lean-fire.title: Lean FIRE Calculator: Retire on a Minimalist Budget
lean-fire.description: Free Lean FIRE calculator: see the smaller portfolio you need when you keep spending low, and how soon a frugal budget gets you there.
lean-fire.lead: Lean FIRE means retiring early on a deliberately small budget. Because your spending is low, your FIRE number is low too, so you can often get there years sooner than a typical plan. This calculator starts from a lean budget and shows what it takes.
how: Your FIRE number scales directly with spending: every extra 1,000 of annual expenses adds about 25,000 to the target at a 4% withdrawal rate. Lean FIRE works by keeping the expense side small through housing, transport and lifestyle choices.

This tool treats annual spending of roughly 25,000 US dollars or less as a lean budget, and scales that line for other currencies. Definitions vary by country and household size, so use the label as a guide, not a rule.
lean-fire.formula: FIRE number = annual expenses ÷ (1 − tax rate) ÷ withdrawal rate.
lean-fire.bestFor: It suits people who are happy with a simple lifestyle, can live in a lower-cost place, or have a partner or household that shares costs.
lean-fire.watchOut: A small budget leaves less room for surprises such as medical bills, home repairs, or inflation in your own spending. Many lean retirees keep a cash buffer or a flexible part-time option.

faq.question: What counts as Lean FIRE?
faq.answer: There is no official line. Many sources describe it as living on a modest budget, and this tool uses about 25,000 US dollars a year as its guide. A single person in a low-cost area and a family in an expensive city will draw the line differently.

faq.question: Is the 4% rule safe for a long lean retirement?
faq.answer: The 4% rule comes from historical studies of 30-year retirements. Early retirees face a longer horizon, so many people test lower rates such as 3.5% in this calculator to see the effect.

faq.question: How can I reach Lean FIRE faster?
faq.answer: Lowering expenses helps twice: it raises the amount you can save each month and it shrinks the target. Try reducing annual expenses by 10% and compare the years to FIRE.

fat-fire.name: Fat FIRE
fat-fire.short: Keep a comfortable lifestyle in early retirement and see the larger target.
fat-fire.title: Fat FIRE Calculator: Retire Early Without Cutting Back
fat-fire.description: Free Fat FIRE calculator: see the portfolio and monthly savings needed to retire early while keeping a comfortable lifestyle.
fat-fire.lead: Fat FIRE is early retirement without major lifestyle cuts, with a larger budget for travel, housing and discretionary spending. The target is bigger, so the plan depends on high savings and long investing. This calculator starts from a high-spending budget and shows the number you are aiming for.
how: Fat FIRE numbers grow quickly. With the defaults here (100,000 US dollars of annual spending, a 4% withdrawal rate and a 15% effective tax rate), the target is about 2.9 million US dollars.

This tool treats annual spending of roughly 100,000 US dollars or more as a fat budget and scales that line for other currencies. The chart shows how long accumulation takes at your monthly contribution, which is the lever that matters most.
fat-fire.formula: FIRE number = annual expenses ÷ (1 − tax rate) ÷ withdrawal rate.
fat-fire.bestFor: It suits high earners who can save a large share of their income for many years and who want a retirement lifestyle close to their working one.
fat-fire.watchOut: A larger portfolio means larger absolute swings in a downturn and often a higher tax bill. Planning for lower withdrawal rates, tax-efficient accounts and flexible spending is common at this level.

faq.question: How much do I need for Fat FIRE?
faq.answer: It depends on your spending. With the defaults here the target is about 2.9 million US dollars, and the calculator recalculates for your own expenses, tax rate and withdrawal rate.

faq.question: Does Fat FIRE need a higher return?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. A higher monthly contribution is usually more reliable than assuming higher returns. Try both to see which changes your timeline more.

faq.question: Is Fat FIRE realistic on a normal income?
faq.answer: It usually requires a high income, a high savings rate, or a long time horizon. Compare it with Lean and Barista FIRE to find the version that fits your situation.

infl.title: Inflation and your FIRE number
infl.tableTitle: FIRE number at different inflation rates
infl.hint: Planning in today's dollars with a real return, as the main calculator does, avoids inflating the target by hand. This tool shows what the same plan looks like in future dollars.

roth.title: Roth vs traditional: after-tax value
roth.hint: With the same return on both sides, only the two tax rates matter: a lower rate later favors traditional, a lower rate now favors Roth. Early retirees often have low taxable income in the years before 59½, which can make a lower future rate realistic.
